STUDY · NEGATIVE RESULT · 16 OCT 2026
  A pre-registered test of volatility-scaled momentum failed its own kill criteria at five positions
  This page reports a negative research result. It is not a strategy, a recommendation or a signal, and nothing on it says what anyone should hold.
  The mechanism passed on 45.7 years of survivorship-free factor data. The version a small account could hold, five long positions with costs charged, failed: no specification passed all four of its kill criteria, so no money was committed.
  Pre-registered 10 Oct 2026 · Run 10 Oct 2026 · Re-run and published 16 Oct 2026 · Script: volmom/ · Data: Kenneth French data library; S&P 500 membership history (fja05680/sp500, MIT); Yahoo monthly closes
  Funding: none. No firm paid for, saw or approved this study. How donttrade is paid →
  Published whether or not the result was interesting. This one was not the result its author hoped for: the test was set up to decide whether a strategy would be used, and it said no.
  ContentsThe short versionWhat was tested, and whyWhat was fixed before any return was computedData and periodMethodResultsWhat this does not showReproduce itReferences
  
  The short version
Volatility-scaled momentum is a published idea (Barroso & Santa-Clara, 2015): take the classic
momentum factor and shrink exposure when its recent volatility is high. Before any return was
computed, I wrote down three specifications, the sample splits, a cost model and seven numeric kill
criteria.
Part A, the mechanism, passed. On 45.7 years of survivorship-free factor data the specification
had never been fitted on, the volatility-scaled version had a Sharpe ratio of 0.78 (t = 5.25)
against 0.37 for plain momentum, and it removed most of the crash risk in the return
distribution.
Part B, the version a small account could hold, failed. With five long positions, a minimum price
and costs charged, no specification passed all four of its kill criteria. Over the same
2013–2026 holdout, simply holding the S&P 500 index fund (SPY) had a higher Sharpe ratio (1.06)
than any of the three specifications (best 0.71). The two specifications that earned high returns
would have hit a 10% drawdown limit 11 and 9 times in 13.75 years. Under the pre-registration,
that meant no money was committed and the result was to be published.
What was tested, and why
The question had two parts, and the second was the one that mattered:

Does scaling momentum by its own recent volatility improve risk-adjusted returns at all?
Does it survive a small retail account’s constraints: five positions, long only, real costs, and a
   10% drawdown limit?

The academic literature answers the first, on long-short portfolios of hundreds of stocks. It does
not answer the second. A pre-registered test with kill criteria set in advance was the way to get an
answer that could not be adjusted after seeing it.
What was fixed before any return was computed

Ranking: 12-1 momentum, the return from 12 months ago to 1 month ago, skipping the latest month.
Parameters: 12% target volatility, 126-trading-day window. These are Barroso & Santa-Clara’s own
  values and were not tuned. No parameter sweep was allowed.
Significance bar: three specifications, Bonferroni-corrected, so nothing counts below
  |t| = 2.394.
Splits, holdout evaluated once: Part A in-sample 1927–1980, holdout Jan 1981 – Aug 2026
  (548 months). Part B in-sample 1997–2012, holdout Jan 2013 – Sep 2026 (165 months).

Data and period

Part A: Kenneth French’s momentum factor and market data, built from CRSP, which keeps delisted
  firms, so this part has no survivorship bias. 1,196 monthly observations from January
  1927 and 26,216 daily observations from November 1926, both to August 2026; no rows dropped in parsing.
Part B: point-in-time S&P 500 membership from fja05680/sp500 (MIT), 2,720 dated snapshots;
  monthly closing prices from Yahoo. Constraints: 5 positions, long only, minimum price $5, and a
  0.20% cost charged on each side of every trade.

Method
Part A uses the published factor directly. Part B rebuilds the strategy from individual stocks each
month, with costs charged on the fraction of the portfolio replaced. Three conventions are worth
knowing before reading the tables:

The Sharpe ratio is not annual return ÷ annual volatility here. Annual return compounds the
  monthly mean; the Sharpe ratio scales it linearly. The two drift apart as the mean grows, which is
  why S2's row in Part A (13.31% return, Sharpe 0.78) does not divide neatly.
Realised volatility is uncentred, sqrt(252 × mean(r²)), which is Barroso & Santa-Clara’s
  published formula. The centred version moves S2's holdout Sharpe from 0.777 to 0.776.
Kurtosis is raw, not excess (a normal distribution has 3).
The 10% drawdown limit was measured, not applied. The pre-registration asked whether the holdout
  would trip it more than three times, so trips are counted on the uninterrupted return series and
  trading never actually stops. That is why a −42.9% drawdown can appear in Part B.

K2 and K3 are defects in the pre-registration, not results. K2 never said which return matrix to use:
in-sample gives 0.7638 (fail), holdout 0.0000 (pass), the common sample 0.0828 (pass). With
only three specifications the statistic has almost no resolution, so it is reported as a range. K3
was written as "≤ 0", but the deflated Sharpe is a probability between 0 and 1, so it could never have
fired. A conventional > 0.95 threshold would pass S2, but that threshold was not pre-registered and is
not used here as a pass.

S1 and S3 earn the returns and fail on drawdown. S2 stays within the limit and loses to the
benchmark. No specification passes everything, so under the pre-registration nothing was traded.
What this does not show

It is not a strategy, a recommendation or a signal, and it is not a recommendation to hold SPY
   or anything else. It is a negative research result. SPY is the benchmark the pre-registration
   named. Beating a strategy over one 13.75-year window is a fact about that window.
Free price data cannot see the stocks that failed. Of 503 current index members, 501 had
   prices (99.6%); of 706 departed members, only 261 did (37.0%). At rebalance dates, median
   index coverage was 52.6% in-sample and 84.8% in the holdout, as printed by the public script on
   fresh downloads on 16 October 2026 (an earlier README figure of 85.0% could not be
   reproduced; see Versions). The missing names are
   disproportionately the ones that went bust, so Part B returns are biased upward. Pricing
   delistings at 0%, −30% (Shumway 1997) or −100% gives identical results, because the missing names
   never enter the panel at all.
The "zero throttling" check on the price download is weak. The fetch logged no rate-limiting,
   but the detector cannot see a batch that silently comes back empty. Some of the missing departed
   names could be missing for that reason rather than because the source lacks them.
2013–2026 was an unusual period for large-cap momentum. A top-5 screen on US large caps over
   that window is largely a concentrated bet on a few mega-cap technology names. 25% a year with a
   −37% drawdown and 11 limit trips looks like a sector bet, not a durable edge.
Part A is not tradeable as measured. It is a long-short factor across hundreds of stocks with
   no costs. Every difference between that and five long positions cuts the same way.
Two forced deviations in Part B. The pre-registration specified daily windows but Part B has
   monthly prices, so S2 uses 12 monthly returns for volatility (noisier, leverage capped at 3×) and
   S3 uses a 10-month average instead of 200 days. Neither was chosen after seeing a result.
Only Part A has a second implementation. Part A was rebuilt from the pre-registration text by
   code written without reading the original computation, and every Part A figure matched. Part B has
   no independent reimplementation.

Reproduce it
Folder: volmom/ in
donttrade/disposition-effect.
pip install -r requirements.txt
python reproduce_volmom.py

Part A takes about a minute. Part B fetches monthly closes for 1,209 tickers on first run (about ten
minutes), then caches them. Both download their own data; no data is shipped in the repository.
On 16 October 2026 the public script was re-run from a clean directory, downloading all of its own
data. Every Part A and Part B figure on this page matched its output.
Since 16 October 2026 the script prints each breakeven cost both per side (0.434%, 0.234%, 0.433%) and
as a round trip (0.868%, 0.467%, 0.866%), and the K7 verdicts S1 pass, S2 fail, S3 pass, matching this
page. Its Part B banner says the 10% limit is counted, not applied (see Versions).
The independent Part A reimplementation, which also produces the K2 range, is in
volmom/verify/:
pip install pandas numpy scipy
python fetch.py
python volmom.py

References

Barroso, P. & Santa-Clara, P. (2015). "Momentum has its moments." Journal of Financial Economics
  116(1), 111–120.
Jegadeesh, N. & Titman, S. (1993). "Returns to Buying Winners and Selling Losers." Journal of
  Finance 48(1), 65–91.
Bailey, D. & López de Prado, M. (2014). "The Deflated Sharpe Ratio." Journal of Portfolio
  Management 40(5).
Shumway, T. (1997). "The Delisting Bias in CRSP Data." Journal of Finance 52(1), 327–340.
Kenneth French data library. fja05680/sp500 (MIT).

Methods and negative results, yes. Live signals, never.

  
  Again: this is a negative research result, not a strategy, a recommendation or a signal. Nothing here says what anyone should buy, sell or hold.
